dx: Wet gangrene of the foot in diabetes with peripheral artery disease
case: A 68-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of swelling, discoloration, and foul-smelling drainage from the second and third toes of his right foot. The symptoms began after a blister formed from new shoes. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years and has calf pain when walking one block. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. The toes are black, moist, and swollen, with purulent drainage, and erythema extends onto the forefoot without a clear line of demarcation. Pedal pulses are not palpable. Ankle-brachial index is 0.48 (normal 1.0 to 1.4). Hemoglobin A1c is 9.6% (normal below 5.7%), and leukocyte count is 16,800/mm3 (normal 4,500 to 11,000). Diagnosis: wet gangrene of the right forefoot.

questions.stem: In patients with arterial occlusion alone, an ischemic toe usually becomes dry, shrunken, and sharply demarcated from viable tissue. Which of the following processes most likely accounts for the moist, swollen, poorly demarcated appearance of this patient's toes?
options: Caseous necrosis from a granulomatous response to mycobacteria
Liquefactive necrosis from bacterial infection and neutrophil enzymes
Coagulative necrosis from arterial occlusion with protein denaturation
Fat necrosis from lipase release and calcium soap formation
approach: Both dry and wet gangrene begin as ischemic coagulative necrosis, so look for what has been added on top.
Fever, pus, leukocytosis, and spreading erythema point to bacterial infection of the dead tissue.
Neutrophil and bacterial enzymes digest the tissue, which is liquefactive necrosis, so the lesion becomes wet and spreads.
questions.why: Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis after arterial occlusion. The tissue mummifies and a clear line separates dead from living tissue. Wet gangrene happens when bacteria invade that dead tissue. Neutrophils and bacterial enzymes then liquefy it, so it becomes moist, swollen, foul smelling, and poorly demarcated, and infection can spread up the limb. Diabetes adds poor blood flow, neuropathy that hides minor injuries, and impaired neutrophil function, which together make this complication more likely.
whyNot: Caseous necrosis is the cheesy necrosis of granulomas in tuberculosis and some fungal infections. It does not cause a wet, purulent toe.
Correct.
Coagulative necrosis is the ischemic process behind both forms of gangrene. On its own it produces dry gangrene, so it does not explain the wet appearance.
Fat necrosis follows lipase release, as in acute pancreatitis or trauma to breast tissue. It is not the process in an infected ischemic toe.

questions.stem: Three years earlier, this patient had osteomyelitis of the calcaneus after a nail went through the rubber sole of his athletic shoe while he was doing yard work. Bone culture at that time most likely grew which of the following organisms?
options: Pasteurella multocida
Salmonella enterica
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
approach: Identify the setting: a puncture wound of the foot through the sole of a shoe.
Recall that the moist foam and rubber inside athletic shoes harbor Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Match the setting to the organism carried in on the nail.
questions.why: A nail passing through a sneaker sole picks up Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which grows in the warm, damp foam of the shoe, and drives it straight into the calcaneus. This is the classic organism for osteomyelitis after a puncture through a shoe sole, and it is also linked to osteomyelitis in people who inject drugs. Pseudomonas is an aerobic, oxidase-positive, gram-negative rod.
whyNot: Pasteurella multocida is the organism for osteomyelitis after a cat or dog bite, carried in from the animal's mouth.
Salmonella is the classic cause of osteomyelitis in people with sickle cell disease, who have poor splenic function and infarcted bone.
Staphylococcus epidermidis causes infection on prosthetic joints and other implanted hardware, where its biofilm protects it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Atherosclerosis and long-standing hyperglycemia have damaged the endothelium of this patient's leg arteries, so it releases less nitric oxide. In normal arteriolar smooth muscle, nitric oxide causes relaxation mainly through which of the following?
options: cGMP-dependent activation of myosin light chain phosphatase
cAMP-dependent inhibition of troponin C calcium binding
IP3-mediated calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Calmodulin-dependent activation of myosin light chain kinase
approach: Nitric oxide diffuses into smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, which makes cGMP.
Smooth muscle contraction depends on phosphorylated myosin light chains, so relaxation needs those phosphates removed.
cGMP-dependent protein kinase lowers cytosolic calcium and activates myosin light chain phosphatase, which removes them.
questions.why: Smooth muscle contracts when calcium binds calmodulin, the complex activates myosin light chain kinase, and the phosphorylated light chain lets myosin cycle on actin. Nitric oxide from endothelium raises cGMP in the smooth muscle cell. cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic calcium and activates myosin light chain phosphatase. The light chains are dephosphorylated and the vessel relaxes. Loss of this signal in diseased arteries favors vasoconstriction and adds to poor flow in peripheral artery disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Smooth muscle has no troponin. Troponin C is the calcium sensor in skeletal and cardiac muscle, and nitric oxide acts through cGMP rather than cAMP.
IP3 releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum after alpha-1 or other Gq receptor activation. That raises calcium and causes contraction.
Calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase is the step that starts smooth muscle contraction, the opposite of what nitric oxide does.

questions.stem: He undergoes a transmetatarsal amputation. Two weeks later, the open stump is filled with red, granular, easily bleeding tissue. Which of the following collagen types is most abundant in the newly formed tissue at this stage?
options: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type VII
approach: Recognize the red, granular, bleeding tissue as granulation tissue in an early healing wound.
Recall that fibroblasts in granulation tissue first lay down a loose collagen meshwork.
That early collagen is type III, which is later replaced by stronger type I as the scar matures.
questions.why: Granulation tissue is new capillaries, fibroblasts, and loose matrix that fills a wound in the first days to weeks. Its fibroblasts first make type III collagen, the thin, flexible collagen of reticular fibers and blood vessel walls. Over weeks to months the scar remodels, and type I collagen replaces most of the type III, which is why tensile strength rises slowly over time.
whyNot: Type I collagen dominates the mature scar, bone, tendon, and ligament. It replaces type III later in healing.
Type II collagen is found in hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus. It is not made in skin wound healing.
Correct.
Type VII collagen forms the anchoring fibrils that attach the epidermis to the dermis. It is defective in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and is not the main collagen of granulation tissue.

dx: Gas gangrene after a contaminated crush injury
case: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 hours after his right lower leg was crushed under farm machinery. A deep laceration on the lateral leg, contaminated with soil, was cleaned and sutured at a local clinic. Since then he has had rapidly increasing, severe pain in the leg. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. The calf and lateral leg are tensely swollen with bronze-to-purple skin, hemorrhagic bullae, a thin, brown, foul-smelling discharge, and crepitus on palpation. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), down from 14.6 g/dL at the time of injury. A radiograph shows gas dissecting along muscle planes. Gram stain of the discharge shows large gram-positive rods with blunt ends and few neutrophils. Diagnosis: gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

questions.stem: Spores of the causative organism are common in soil, yet most contaminated surface wounds never develop this infection. Which of the following features of this wound most directly allowed the spores to germinate and multiply?
options: Large numbers of neutrophils recruited into the injured muscle
Exposed collagen fibers in the torn fascial layers
Low oxidation-reduction potential in devitalized muscle
High glucose concentration in the wound exudate
approach: Identify the organism as Clostridium perfringens, a spore-forming obligate anaerobe.
Spores germinate only where oxygen tension and redox potential are low.
A deep crush wound with dead muscle, poor blood supply, and soil, then closed with sutures, creates exactly that environment.
questions.why: Clostridium perfringens spores sit harmlessly in soil and on skin. They germinate only in an anaerobic setting. Crushed, devitalized muscle has no blood flow, foreign material uses up oxygen, and closing the wound seals it off. Once growing, the organism releases toxins that kill nearby muscle and lower the redox potential further, so the infection spreads through muscle within hours, with gas, severe pain, bronze skin, hemolysis, and shock.
whyNot: Neutrophils fight infection. In gas gangrene the toxins actually destroy neutrophils, which is why the Gram stain shows few of them.
Exposed collagen helps organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus adhere. It does not create the anaerobic conditions spores need to germinate.
Correct.
Glucose supports bacterial growth in many settings, but it does not trigger germination of anaerobic spores. Low oxygen is the key requirement.

questions.stem: His hemoglobin fell from 14.6 to 8.9 g/dL in 30 hours without external bleeding. Which of the following actions of the organism's major toxin best explains both the hemolysis and the muscle necrosis?
options: Hydrolysis of phosphatidylcholine in host cell membranes
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 in host cells
Cleavage of SNARE proteins at presynaptic nerve terminals
Cross-linking of MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors
approach: Identify the main toxin of Clostridium perfringens as alpha toxin.
Alpha toxin is a phospholipase C, also called lecithinase.
Breaking down membrane lecithin lyses any cell it reaches, including red cells and muscle fibers.
questions.why: Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a phospholipase C that splits phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) and sphingomyelin in cell membranes. Red cells lyse, which explains the falling hemoglobin. Muscle fibers, endothelial cells, and leukocytes are destroyed, which explains the myonecrosis, the spreading edema, and the scarce neutrophils. The same lecithinase activity is the basis of the Nagler reaction on egg yolk agar in the laboratory.
whyNot: Correct.
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 stops protein synthesis. This is how diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A kill cells.
SNARE cleavage blocks neurotransmitter release. This is how tetanus and botulinum toxins act, made by other clostridia.
Cross-linking MHC class II to T-cell receptors is the action of superantigens such as toxic shock syndrome toxin from Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.stem: Surgical exploration shows that the laceration severed the nerve running through the lateral compartment of the leg, between the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis muscles. Which of the following deficits is most likely to result from this nerve injury?
options: Weak dorsiflexion with numbness limited to the first web space
Weak eversion with numbness over the dorsum of the foot
Weak plantarflexion with numbness over the sole of the foot
Weak knee extension with numbness over the medial leg
approach: Name the nerve of the lateral compartment: the superficial fibular nerve.
Its muscles, fibularis longus and brevis, evert the foot.
Its skin territory is most of the dorsum of the foot, sparing the first web space.
questions.why: The common fibular nerve splits at the neck of the fibula. The superficial branch runs in the lateral compartment and supplies fibularis longus and brevis, the main evertors of the foot. It then becomes cutaneous and supplies most of the dorsum of the foot. Cutting it weakens eversion and numbs the dorsum, while dorsiflexion is preserved because the deep fibular nerve in the anterior compartment is intact.
whyNot: This is a deep fibular nerve injury, which affects the anterior compartment dorsiflexors and the skin of the first web space.
Correct.
This is a tibial nerve injury. The tibial nerve runs in the posterior compartment and supplies the plantarflexors and the sole.
This is a femoral nerve injury in the thigh, which weakens the quadriceps and numbs the medial leg through the saphenous nerve.

questions.stem: Serum creatine kinase (reference 40 to 200 U/L) and potassium (reference 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L) are measured on arrival. Which of the following sets of results is most likely?
options: Creatine kinase 120 U/L; potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Creatine kinase 120 U/L; potassium 6.4 mEq/L
Creatine kinase 21,000 U/L; potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Creatine kinase 21,000 U/L; potassium 6.4 mEq/L
approach: Recognize widespread muscle necrosis from the crush injury and the toxin as rhabdomyolysis.
Dying muscle releases its intracellular contents: creatine kinase, potassium, phosphate, and myoglobin.
Expect a very high creatine kinase with hyperkalemia.
questions.why: Muscle cells hold large amounts of creatine kinase and most of the body's potassium. When many fibers die, as with a crush injury and clostridial myonecrosis, both leak into the blood. Creatine kinase rises to many times normal, and potassium climbs, which can cause fatal arrhythmias. Hemolysis here adds more potassium. Released myoglobin also reaches the kidney, where it can cause acute kidney injury, and it turns the urine dipstick positive for blood without red cells on microscopy.
whyNot: A normal creatine kinase rules out major muscle necrosis, and a low potassium is the opposite of what cell breakdown produces.
Hyperkalemia fits, but a normal creatine kinase is not possible with this much dead muscle.
The creatine kinase fits, but necrotic muscle and lysed red cells release potassium, so it rises rather than falls.
Correct.

dx: Salmonella osteomyelitis in a child with sickle cell disease
case: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (hemoglobin SS) is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of fever and pain above his left knee. He has refused to bear weight for 2 days. Two weeks ago he had 3 days of diarrhea. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. The distal left thigh is warm, swollen, and tender. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL (his baseline is 8.0 g/dL), leukocyte count is 19,500/mm3 (normal 5,000 to 14,500), and C-reactive protein is 9.2 mg/dL (normal below 1.0). MRI shows marrow edema in the distal femoral metaphysis with a small subperiosteal collection. Blood cultures grow gram-negative rods that do not ferment lactose and produce hydrogen sulfide. Diagnosis: Salmonella osteomyelitis of the distal femur.

questions.stem: In children, hematogenous osteomyelitis most often begins in the metaphysis of a long bone, as in this patient. Which of the following features of the growing bone best explains this location?
options: Rich supply of epiphyseal arteries crossing the open growth plate
High density of osteoclasts along the diaphyseal endosteum
Exposure of the metaphyseal cortex inside the joint capsule
Slow flow in looping capillaries beneath the growth plate
approach: Recall the blood supply of the metaphysis in a child: nutrient artery branches end in hairpin loops near the growth plate.
These loops open into wide sinusoidal veins where blood flow slows sharply.
Bacteria in the blood settle where flow is slow and phagocytes are few, so infection starts there.
questions.why: In a growing long bone, branches of the nutrient artery run up to the growth plate, turn back in tight loops, and empty into large venous sinusoids. Blood slows down in these sinusoids, and the area has few phagocytes and gaps in the vessel lining. Circulating bacteria lodge there and multiply. After infancy the growth plate blocks spread into the epiphysis, so the infection stays in the metaphysis or tracks out under the periosteum, as in this boy. In sickle cell disease, bone infarcts can also seed infection in the diaphysis.
whyNot: After infancy, vessels do not cross the growth plate. The plate acts as a barrier, which is why childhood infection stays on the metaphyseal side.
Osteoclasts resorb bone, but they do not trap circulating bacteria. Their activity does not explain where infection starts.
In some joints, such as the hip, the metaphysis lies inside the capsule. That explains spread into the joint, but not why infection starts in the metaphysis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why children with this patient's underlying disease are especially prone to invasive infection with this organism?
options: Deficiency of terminal complement components
Splenic dysfunction from repeated infarction
Selective deficiency of secretory IgA
Thymic hypoplasia with low T-cell counts
approach: Link the setting: osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella in sickle cell disease.
Recall that sickled cells infarct the spleen early in childhood, leaving functional asplenia.
Without a working spleen, bacteremia from the gut is cleared poorly and seeds infarcted bone.
questions.why: Repeated sickling in the spleen causes infarction, so most children with hemoglobin SS have little splenic function by early childhood. The spleen normally filters bacteria from the blood and makes opsonizing antibody. Salmonella can enter from the gut, sometimes through areas of bowel injured by sickling, and without splenic clearance it reaches the bone. Infarcted bone with poor blood flow gives it a place to grow. This is why Salmonella is a classic cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease, alongside Staphylococcus aureus.
whyNot: Terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9) causes recurrent Neisseria infections. It is not part of sickle cell disease.
Correct.
IgA deficiency causes sinus and lung infections and Giardia diarrhea. It does not explain Salmonella bone infection in sickle cell disease.
Thymic hypoplasia, as in DiGeorge syndrome, causes viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections from low T cells. It is not linked to sickle cell disease.

topics: Functional asplenia in sickle cell disease

questions.stem: In children without sickle cell disease, hematogenous osteomyelitis is most often caused by gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase and coagulase positive. Which of the following virulence factors most directly allows that organism to attach to exposed bone matrix?
options: Protein A that binds the Fc portion of IgG antibodies
M protein that blocks complement deposition on the cell
Surface adhesins that bind collagen and fibronectin
Superantigen toxin that activates T cells nonspecifically
approach: Identify the organism as Staphylococcus aureus.
Separate its virulence factors by job: attachment, immune evasion, or toxin effects.
Attachment to bone depends on surface adhesins that bind the matrix proteins collagen and fibronectin.
questions.why: Staphylococcus aureus carries surface proteins that bind host matrix molecules, including collagen-binding and fibronectin-binding adhesins. These let it stick to bone matrix and to injured tissue, which is a key reason it is the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis. Once attached, it can form biofilm, especially on hardware, which shields it from antibiotics and phagocytes.
whyNot: Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG so the antibody cannot opsonize the bacterium. It helps evade phagocytosis, not attach to bone.
M protein is a virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes, which is catalase negative and grows in chains.
Correct.
Superantigens such as toxic shock syndrome toxin cause massive cytokine release and shock. They do not mediate attachment to bone.

questions.stem: Treatment is delayed, and 3 months later he has a draining sinus over the distal thigh. Radiographs show a dense, sharply separated fragment of cortical bone lying in a cavity, surrounded by a shell of new subperiosteal bone. Which of the following best describes the dense fragment and its significance?
options: Sequestrum; avascular dead bone that shields bacteria from drugs
Involucrum; reactive periosteal new bone that walls off the infected site
Brodie abscess; a walled-off cavity with a sclerotic bony rim
Bone infarct; sterile necrosis from sickling that later calcifies
approach: Separate the two structures in chronic osteomyelitis: the dead fragment and the new bone shell around it.
The dense, separated fragment is dead bone, the sequestrum, and the shell is the involucrum.
Dead bone has no blood supply, so antibiotics and leukocytes cannot reach bacteria inside it, and it usually must be removed.
questions.why: In chronic osteomyelitis, pus under the periosteum strips away the blood supply of a piece of cortex, and that piece dies and separates. This dead fragment is the sequestrum. The lifted periosteum lays down a shell of new bone, the involucrum, around it. Because the sequestrum has no blood flow, antibiotics and immune cells cannot reach the bacteria living on it, so surgical removal is usually needed for cure. A draining sinus is common, and years of drainage can lead to squamous cell carcinoma in the tract.
whyNot: Correct.
The involucrum is the shell of new bone in this film, not the dense fragment inside it.
A Brodie abscess is a localized subacute abscess, usually in the metaphysis, with a sclerotic rim and no separated dead fragment.
Sickle cell disease does cause bone infarcts, but a fragment lying in a cavity with an involucrum and a draining sinus is infected dead bone.

case: A 41-year-old woman who moved to the United States 3 years ago from a region where tuberculosis is endemic comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive mid-back pain, night sweats, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Examination shows a sharp, angular kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction with point tenderness over T11 and T12. She holds the right hip slightly flexed, and passive extension of the hip is painful. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 64 mm/h (normal 0 to 20). An interferon-gamma release assay is positive. MRI shows destruction of the T11 and T12 vertebral bodies, narrowing of the disc between them, and a right psoas abscess. CT-guided biopsy shows caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli. Diagnosis: tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease).

questions.stem: A chest radiograph shows a small calcified peripheral lung nodule and a calcified hilar lymph node, with no cavities or active lung disease. Which of the following best describes how the organism most likely reached her vertebrae?
options: Hematogenous spread from an earlier lung infection
Direct extension from a pulmonary cavity through the pleura
Ingestion of organisms with spread through the portal vein
Direct inoculation during an earlier spinal procedure
approach: Recognize the calcified nodule and hilar node as a healed primary (Ghon) complex.
During primary infection, Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters the blood and seeds distant organs, where it can stay dormant for years.
Vertebral bodies, with their rich marrow blood flow, are a common site, and reactivation later causes Pott disease.
questions.why: In primary tuberculosis, bacilli spread from the lung to the hilar nodes and then into the blood, seeding many organs. Most foci are walled off by granulomas and stay dormant. Years later, a vertebral focus can reactivate. Caseating granulomas destroy the front of the vertebral bodies next to the disc, the infection spreads under the anterior longitudinal ligament to the next vertebra, and the bodies collapse forward into a gibbus. Pus tracking down along the psoas forms a psoas abscess, which explains her painful hip extension.
whyNot: Correct.
Direct extension needs active disease next to the spine. Her lungs show only healed calcified lesions with no cavity.
Swallowed organisms cause intestinal tuberculosis. Portal blood drains to the liver and is not how the spine is seeded.
Direct inoculation causes infection only after surgery or injection into the spine, and she has had no such procedure.

questions.stem: The infection began in the T12 vertebral body next to the disc it shares with T11. During embryonic development, the T12 vertebral body formed from which of the following?
options: One whole sclerotome lying at the level of the twelfth spinal nerve
Cranial halves of two adjacent sclerotomes joined across a disc
Caudal half of one sclerotome joined to cranial half of the next
Paraxial dermomyotome cells that migrate around the neural tube
approach: Recall that vertebral bodies come from sclerotome, while dermomyotome forms dermis and muscle.
Each sclerotome splits into a cranial and a caudal half.
In resegmentation, the caudal half of one sclerotome fuses with the cranial half of the next to form one vertebral body.
questions.why: Sclerotome cells from the somites surround the notochord and neural tube. Each sclerotome splits into halves, and every vertebral body forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome joined to the cranial half of the one below. Because of this shift, each vertebra spans two body segments, the segmental muscles from the myotomes bridge the disc and can move one vertebra on the next, and the spinal nerves exit near the discs. The notochord between the bodies persists as the nucleus pulposus.
whyNot: A vertebral body does not come from a single whole sclerotome. Resegmentation combines halves of two sclerotomes.
The halves that fuse are a caudal half and a cranial half. Two cranial halves do not join.
Correct.
Dermomyotome forms dermis and skeletal muscle. Vertebrae come from sclerotome.

questions.stem: Which of the following immune mechanisms is mainly responsible for the caseating granulomas and the destruction of her vertebral bodies?
options: Type I, IgE-mediated degranulation of tissue mast cells and basophils
Type II, IgG antibodies binding antigens fixed on the cell surface
Type III, deposition of immune complexes that activate complement
Type IV, Th1 cell activation of macrophages by interferon-gamma
approach: Granulomas form when T cells repeatedly activate macrophages against an antigen they cannot clear.
This T cell driven response is delayed-type, or type IV, hypersensitivity.
The positive interferon-gamma release assay shows the same Th1 memory response.
questions.why: Macrophages that ingest Mycobacterium tuberculosis present its antigens and release IL-12, which drives CD4 T cells to become Th1 cells. Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill bacilli and to form epithelioid cells and giant cells, building a granuloma. TNF helps hold the granuloma together. The central caseous necrosis and much of the bone destruction come from this host response rather than from bacterial toxins, which is the type IV hypersensitivity pattern.
whyNot: Type I hypersensitivity causes allergy and anaphylaxis within minutes. It does not form granulomas.
Type II hypersensitivity is antibody against cell or tissue antigens, as in the polyarthritis of rheumatic fever and in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Type III hypersensitivity is immune complex disease, as in the arthritis of SLE. It causes vasculitis and complement-driven inflammation, not caseating granulomas.
Correct.

questions.stem: In adults, both tuberculous and pyogenic vertebral infections typically involve two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them, as in this patient. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: The adult disc has a rich blood supply that seeds the bones on either side
A single segmental artery supplies endplates on both sides of a disc
Infection begins in the posterior arch and spreads forward into the bodies
Organisms spread through the spinal canal from the epidural space
approach: Recall that the adult intervertebral disc is avascular, so bacteria cannot lodge in it first.
Blood-borne organisms settle in the richly supplied bone just under the vertebral endplates.
Branches of one segmental artery supply the endplates above and below a disc, so both vertebrae are seeded and the disc is destroyed between them.
questions.why: In adults the disc has no blood vessels and gets nutrients by diffusion. Bacteria arriving in the blood therefore lodge in the vascular bone beside the endplates. A segmental artery divides to supply the lower endplate of one vertebra and the upper endplate of the next, so the infection usually involves both bodies and then spreads into the disc between them. This differs from children, where hematogenous osteomyelitis favors the metaphyses of long bones, and from diabetic foot osteomyelitis, which spreads directly from a skin ulcer.
whyNot: The adult disc is avascular. Infection reaches it from the bone on either side, not the reverse.
Correct.
Vertebral osteomyelitis starts in the vascular vertebral bodies. The posterior arch is usually spared until late.
Epidural abscess is a complication that spreads from the infected bodies. It is not the starting point.

case: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 10-day history of muscle pain, fever, and swelling around his eyes. Three weeks ago he ate homemade pork sausage made from a pig raised and slaughtered on a neighbor's farm, and a few days later he had abdominal cramps and diarrhea for 3 days. His calves, thighs, shoulders, and jaw muscles ache, and chewing is painful. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral periorbital edema, subconjunctival hemorrhages, splinter hemorrhages, and tender proximal and calf muscles. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm3 (normal 4,500 to 11,000) with 32% eosinophils (normal 1 to 4%). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 46 mm/h (normal 0 to 20), and serum creatine kinase is 2,850 U/L (normal 40 to 200). Serologic testing confirms the diagnosis of trichinellosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following stages of the parasite's life cycle is mainly responsible for this patient's current muscle symptoms?
options: Adult worms in the intestinal mucosa releasing eggs in the stool
Eggs hatching in the duodenum with larvae migrating through the liver
Newborn larvae encysting within skeletal muscle cells
Larvae penetrating the skin and migrating to the lungs
approach: Lay out the timeline: diarrhea in the first week (intestinal phase), then muscle pain from the second week on (muscle phase).
Recall that Trichinella spiralis females are viviparous and release live larvae, not eggs.
Those larvae travel in the blood to skeletal muscle, enter muscle cells, and encyst, causing myositis.
questions.why: A person is infected by eating encysted larvae in undercooked pork or game. Stomach acid frees the larvae, which mature into adults in the small intestine and cause the early diarrhea. About a week later, females release newborn larvae that enter lymph and blood and invade striated muscle. Each larva enters a muscle cell and turns it into a nurse cell, where it coils and encysts. This muscle invasion causes myalgia, high creatine kinase, eosinophilia, and the periorbital edema and splinter hemorrhages of the systemic phase.
whyNot: Trichinella females release live larvae, and eggs are not passed in the stool. The intestinal stage also explains the early diarrhea, not the muscle pain.
Egg hatching with migration through the liver and lungs describes Ascaris. Trichinella has no free egg stage.
Correct.
Skin penetration with lung migration is how hookworms and Strongyloides infect people. Trichinella is acquired by eating meat.

questions.stem: A deltoid muscle biopsy shows coiled larvae inside host cells. The larvae also invade cardiac muscle, but they do not encyst there. Which of the following features of the surrounding uninfected fibers identifies the tissue as skeletal muscle rather than cardiac muscle?
options: Central nuclei with intercalated discs between cells
Fusiform cells with dense bodies and no striations
Branched cells joined end to end by gap junctions
Multinucleated fibers with nuclei at the periphery
approach: List the histologic features that separate the three muscle types.
Skeletal muscle fibers are long, unbranched, and multinucleated, with nuclei pushed to the edge.
Cardiac muscle has central nuclei, branching, and intercalated discs; smooth muscle has no striations.
questions.why: Skeletal muscle fibers form by fusion of many myoblasts, so each fiber has many nuclei, and these sit just under the sarcolemma at the periphery. The fibers are striated and do not branch. Cardiac muscle cells are single cells with one or two central nuclei, they branch, and they join end to end at intercalated discs that contain gap junctions and desmosomes. Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped, with one central nucleus, dense bodies, and no striations.
whyNot: Central nuclei and intercalated discs identify cardiac muscle.
Fusiform cells with dense bodies and no striations describe smooth muscle.
Branching cells linked by gap junctions describe cardiac muscle, which conducts electrical impulses from cell to cell.
Correct.

topics: Histology of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle

questions.stem: Before serologic results were available, his physician considered polymyalgia rheumatica because of his muscle pain and stiffness. Which of the following findings from this case most strongly argues against polymyalgia rheumatica?
options: Serum creatine kinase of 2,850 U/L
Age of 58 years
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/h
Tenderness of the shoulder and thigh muscles
approach: Recall what polymyalgia rheumatica looks like: adults over 50, girdle pain and stiffness, high ESR, and normal muscle enzymes.
Its inflammation is in the bursae and synovium around the shoulders and hips, so muscle fibers are not damaged.
A high creatine kinase means myofiber necrosis, which points to myositis and away from polymyalgia rheumatica.
questions.why: Creatine kinase leaks from damaged muscle fibers. In polymyalgia rheumatica the inflammation sits in the bursae and joints around the shoulder and hip girdles, so creatine kinase stays normal and strength is preserved. Inflammatory myositis, whether autoimmune or parasitic as here, damages muscle fibers and raises creatine kinase, often many times above normal. A muscle biopsy in myositis shows inflammatory cells and necrotic fibers, while biopsy is normal in polymyalgia rheumatica.
whyNot: Correct.
Polymyalgia rheumatica occurs in adults over 50, so his age fits the diagnosis.
An elevated ESR is expected in polymyalgia rheumatica and does not argue against it.
Pain around the shoulder and hip girdles is the main complaint in polymyalgia rheumatica, so this finding fits both diagnoses.

questions.stem: He is treated with albendazole and a 2-month tapering course of high-dose prednisone. Four months later, his muscle pain is gone, but he has trouble rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Serum creatine kinase is 95 U/L. Which of the following findings is most likely on a muscle biopsy now?
options: Perifascicular atrophy with perivascular inflammation
Selective atrophy of type II fibers without inflammation
Grouped atrophy with large clusters of a single fiber type
Endomysial CD8 T cells invading nonnecrotic fibers
approach: Note the new proximal weakness after weeks of high-dose glucocorticoids, with a normal creatine kinase.
Normal creatine kinase argues against active myofiber necrosis or inflammation.
Glucocorticoids cause a myopathy marked by atrophy of type II (fast, glycolytic) fibers.
questions.why: High-dose glucocorticoids break down muscle protein and reduce protein synthesis, and type II fibers are hit hardest. The result is proximal weakness with a normal creatine kinase and a biopsy showing small type II fibers without inflammation or necrosis. Disuse causes the same type II atrophy. Neurogenic disease looks different: denervated fibers become reinnervated by neighboring motor units, producing fiber type grouping and grouped atrophy, often with fasciculations.
whyNot: Perifascicular atrophy with perivascular inflammation is the pattern of dermatomyositis, which has a high creatine kinase and skin findings.
Correct.
Grouped atrophy and fiber type grouping mean denervation and reinnervation, as in spinal muscular atrophy or motor neuron disease.
CD8 T cells invading fibers is the pattern of polymyositis, which raises creatine kinase.

dx: Tibial shaft fracture with anterior compartment syndrome
case: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle collision. Radiographs show a closed, displaced fracture of the right tibial shaft, and the leg is splinted. Eight hours later she has severe, increasing pain in the front of the leg that is not relieved by intravenous opioids. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. The anterior leg is tense and firm. Passive plantarflexion of the toes causes severe pain. The dorsalis pedis pulse is 2+ and capillary refill is normal. Sensation is decreased in the first web space of the foot. Anterior compartment pressure is 48 mm Hg (normal below 10). Diagnosis: acute compartment syndrome of the anterior compartment of the leg.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the muscles in this compartment are ischemic even though the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable?
options: Bone fragments have partly torn the anterior tibial artery wall
Tissue pressure collapses capillaries and veins but not arteries
Reflex spasm of the femoral artery has reduced inflow to the limb
Marrow fat emboli have occluded arterioles within the muscle
approach: Compare pressures: compartment pressure 48 mm Hg, arterial systolic pressure about 128 mm Hg.
Capillary and venous pressures are far lower, roughly 10 to 30 mm Hg, so they are overcome first.
Blood still flows through the large artery to the foot, but the muscle capillaries collapse and the tissue becomes ischemic.
questions.why: Bleeding and edema from the fracture fill a closed fascial compartment that cannot expand. As pressure rises above venous and capillary pressure, venous outflow and capillary flow stop, while the main artery, with far higher pressure, stays open. The muscle and nerves in the compartment become ischemic even though the distal pulse is normal. That is why severe pain, pain with passive stretch, and sensory changes appear early, and loss of pulse is a late and unreliable sign. Untreated, the dead muscle scars and contracts into a Volkmann ischemic contracture.
whyNot: A torn artery would reduce or abolish the distal pulse and would cause ischemia of the whole foot, not just one compartment.
Correct.
Femoral artery spasm would reduce flow to the entire limb and weaken the distal pulse. It would not single out the anterior compartment.
Fat embolism after long bone fractures mainly affects the lungs, brain, and skin. It does not produce a tense, painful compartment.

questions.stem: If the compartment pressure is not relieved, injury to the nerve running through this compartment is most likely to cause which of the following motor deficits?
options: Loss of ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension
Loss of foot eversion with intact dorsiflexion
Loss of plantarflexion and foot inversion
Loss of knee extension and the patellar reflex
approach: Name the nerve of the anterior compartment: the deep fibular nerve, which runs with the anterior tibial artery.
Its numb skin area, the first web space, is already affected in this patient.
The muscles it supplies, tibialis anterior and the long toe extensors, dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes, so their loss causes foot drop.
questions.why: The deep fibular nerve runs in the anterior compartment and supplies tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and fibularis tertius. These muscles dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes. Its only skin area on the dorsum is the first web space. Ischemic damage to this nerve and these muscles leaves a foot drop with a high-stepping gait, which is a common lasting result of untreated anterior compartment syndrome.
whyNot: Correct.
Isolated loss of eversion follows superficial fibular nerve injury in the lateral compartment.
Loss of plantarflexion and inversion follows tibial nerve injury in the posterior compartment.
Loss of knee extension and the patellar reflex follows femoral nerve injury in the thigh.

topics: Deep fibular nerve and foot drop

questions.stem: She undergoes fasciotomy and intramedullary nailing of the tibia. She smokes one pack of cigarettes daily and continues to smoke after surgery. Five months later, radiographs show a persistent fracture line with little bridging bone. Which of the following steps of fracture healing was most likely impaired?
options: Formation of the initial hematoma around the fracture ends
Recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the site
Osteoclast remodeling of woven bone into lamellar bone
Vascular ingrowth that converts cartilage callus to bone
approach: Sequence healing: hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, then remodeling.
No bridging bone at 5 months means the soft callus has not turned into hard bony callus.
That conversion needs new blood vessels, which smoking and damaged surrounding muscle both reduce.
questions.why: Fracture healing starts with a hematoma and inflammation in the first days. Over the next weeks, a soft callus of granulation tissue, fibrocartilage, and cartilage bridges the gap. New blood vessels then grow into this callus, and osteoblasts replace the cartilage with woven bone, forming the hard callus. Months to years of remodeling turn woven bone into lamellar bone. Nicotine constricts vessels and slows angiogenesis, and the muscle injury from compartment syndrome reduces local blood supply, so the step that depends on blood vessels fails and union is delayed. Infection, instability, diabetes, and malnutrition also delay healing.
whyNot: The hematoma forms within hours of the fracture. Smoking does not stop it from forming.
Inflammatory cell recruitment happens in the first days and is not the step that leaves a gap without bone at 5 months.
Remodeling acts on bone that has already bridged the gap. Here no bridging bone has formed.
Correct.

questions.stem: While the compartment pressure was high, oxygen delivery to the anterior compartment muscles fell sharply. After stored phosphocreatine was used up, which of the following processes allowed these muscle cells to keep making ATP?
options: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria
Oxidation of ketone bodies through the citric acid cycle
Conversion of pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+
Release of free glucose from glycogen by glucose-6-phosphatase
approach: Without oxygen, the electron transport chain stops, so all mitochondrial fuel oxidation stops.
Glycolysis can still make ATP, but it needs NAD+ to keep running.
Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate and regenerates NAD+, so anaerobic glycolysis continues.
questions.why: Muscle first uses its small store of phosphocreatine, which creatine kinase converts to ATP within seconds. After that, without oxygen, it relies on anaerobic glycolysis of glucose and its own glycogen. Glycolysis makes 2 ATP per glucose but uses NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and regenerates that NAD+, so glycolysis keeps going. Lactate builds up, the tissue becomes acidic, and the output is far too low to keep the muscle alive for long.
whyNot: Beta-oxidation feeds acetyl-CoA and NADH to mitochondria, which need oxygen to make ATP. It stops in ischemia.
Ketone oxidation also depends on the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, which require oxygen.
Correct.
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. It breaks glycogen down to glucose-6-phosphate and uses it inside the cell rather than releasing free glucose.

dx: Supracondylar humerus fracture in a child
case: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she fell from playground monkey bars onto her outstretched right hand with the elbow extended. She has severe elbow pain and will not move the arm. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. The right elbow is markedly swollen with an S-shaped deformity of the distal arm. The right radial pulse is faint compared with the left, and capillary refill in the fingers is 3 seconds (normal 2 seconds or less). Radiographs show a completely displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus with the distal fragment displaced posteriorly and laterally. Diagnosis: displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the right humerus.

questions.stem: If the compression of the brachial artery is not relieved, which of the following is the most likely long-term complication in this patient's limb?
options: Avascular necrosis of the proximal humeral fracture fragment
Fat embolism syndrome with hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae
Nonunion from interruption of a retrograde intraosseous blood supply
Fixed wrist and finger flexion from forearm muscle fibrosis
approach: Recognize the faint radial pulse as compromise of the brachial artery by the displaced fracture.
Prolonged poor flow, often with swelling, causes ischemia of the deep forearm flexor muscles.
Dead muscle is replaced by scar that shortens, leaving the wrist and fingers fixed in flexion: Volkmann ischemic contracture.
questions.why: In an extension-type supracondylar fracture, the sharp end of the proximal fragment can kink or tear the brachial artery in the front of the elbow. Ischemia, often with forearm compartment syndrome, kills the deep flexor muscles, especially flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus. Fibrous scar then replaces and shortens them, producing Volkmann ischemic contracture with a clawed, flexed wrist and fingers. Restoring flow quickly prevents it.
whyNot: Avascular necrosis from a disrupted blood supply is typical of femoral neck fractures and of the proximal scaphoid, not the distal humerus in a child.
Fat embolism syndrome follows fractures of large long bones such as the femur, mostly in adults. It does not follow arterial compression.
Nonunion from a retrograde blood supply is the classic risk of scaphoid waist fractures. Supracondylar fractures in children heal well.
Correct.

questions.stem: With the distal fragment displaced posterolaterally, the sharp end of the proximal fragment is driven forward and medially into the cubital fossa, where it compresses the brachial artery. Injury to the nerve that runs beside this artery would most likely cause which of the following deficits?
options: Inability to extend the wrist and fingers
Weak elbow flexion with numbness of the lateral forearm
Inability to oppose the thumb and flex the index fingertip
Weak finger abduction with clawing of the ring and little fingers
approach: Recall the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial: biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.
The nerve beside the brachial artery is the median nerve, so a medially driven spike threatens both.
Median nerve injury at the elbow weakens thumb opposition and flexion of the thumb and index finger.
questions.why: In the cubital fossa, the median nerve lies just medial to the brachial artery, which lies medial to the biceps tendon. When the distal fragment shifts posterolaterally, the proximal fragment pushes into these medial structures. Median nerve injury at this level weakens the thenar muscles, so the thumb cannot oppose, and weakens flexor pollicis longus and the index part of flexor digitorum profundus through the anterior interosseous branch, so the child cannot make an OK sign. Posteromedial displacement instead puts the radial nerve at risk.
whyNot: Wrist drop comes from radial nerve injury, which is more likely when the distal fragment shifts posteromedially.
Weak elbow flexion with lateral forearm numbness comes from musculocutaneous nerve injury, which is rare in this fracture.
Correct.
Clawing of the ring and little fingers with weak finger abduction comes from ulnar nerve injury, more typical of flexion-type fractures or medial pin placement.

topics: Median nerve injury at the elbow

questions.stem: At follow-up after reduction and pinning, the physician taps the biceps tendon to test the reflex. Which of the following receptors and spinal cord segments carry the afferent limb of this reflex?
options: Golgi tendon organ, Ib afferent, C5 to C6
Muscle spindle, Ia afferent, C5 to C6
Golgi tendon organ, Ib afferent, C7
Muscle spindle, Ia afferent, C7
approach: A tendon tap briefly stretches the muscle, which is the stimulus for the muscle spindle.
Spindle Ia afferents synapse directly on alpha motor neurons, producing a monosynaptic stretch reflex.
The biceps reflex is carried by C5 and C6; the triceps reflex by C7.
questions.why: Tapping the biceps tendon stretches the muscle quickly. Muscle spindles, which lie parallel to the muscle fibers, sense this stretch and fire through large Ia afferents. These synapse directly on alpha motor neurons for the biceps in the C5 and C6 segments, and the muscle contracts. Golgi tendon organs sit in series with the muscle at the tendon junction and sense tension through Ib afferents, which inhibit the same muscle rather than produce a brisk jerk.
whyNot: The segments are right, but Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the muscle. They do not drive the tendon jerk.
Correct.
Golgi tendon organs do not mediate the stretch reflex, and C7 carries the triceps reflex.
The receptor is right, but C7 is the root for the triceps reflex. The biceps reflex is C5 to C6.

topics: Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs

questions.stem: While the brachial artery was compressed, her forearm muscles relied on anaerobic glycolysis and released lactate. After blood flow is restored, which of the following best describes the main fate of this lactate?
options: Converted to glucose in the liver, at a net cost of ATP
Converted to glucose in skeletal muscle for glycogen storage
Excreted unchanged by the kidneys as the main route of clearance
Converted to alanine in the liver and returned to muscle
approach: Lactate from muscle travels in the blood to the liver.
The liver turns it back into pyruvate and then into glucose by gluconeogenesis, which returns to muscle. This loop is the Cori cycle.
Making glucose costs more ATP in the liver than anaerobic glycolysis gave the muscle, so the cycle has a net energy cost.
questions.why: In the Cori cycle, muscle converts glucose to lactate and gains 2 ATP per glucose. The liver takes up the lactate, converts it to pyruvate with lactate dehydrogenase, and builds glucose by gluconeogenesis at a cost of 6 ATP equivalents per glucose. The glucose returns to muscle. The cycle therefore costs the body about 4 ATP per turn, but it keeps glycolysis going in muscle and prevents lactate from piling up in the blood.
whyNot: Correct.
Skeletal muscle does not carry out meaningful gluconeogenesis and lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot make free glucose from lactate.
Only a small amount of lactate is lost in urine. The liver, and to a lesser degree the kidney cortex, clears most of it by metabolism.
The alanine cycle runs the other way: muscle sends alanine to the liver, which uses it to make glucose.

case: A 19-year-old man who plays college soccer comes to the physician because of a firm, painful lump in his right thigh. Five weeks ago an opponent's knee struck the front of his thigh, causing a large bruise and swelling. Since then the pain has lessened, but the lump has grown harder and he cannot fully bend his knee. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a 6-cm firm, mildly tender mass deep in the anterior mid-thigh. Knee flexion is limited to 90 degrees (normal about 135 degrees). A radiograph shows a well-circumscribed mass within the quadriceps with a rim of mineralization at its periphery and a lucent center, separated from the femoral cortex by a thin radiolucent line. Diagnosis: myositis ossificans of the vastus intermedius.

questions.stem: Because the lesion is growing in a young adult, a biopsy is considered to exclude osteosarcoma. Which of the following histologic patterns would most strongly support myositis ossificans?
options: Malignant cells laying down osteoid that invades the surrounding muscle
Mature bone centrally with atypical cells infiltrating at the margins
Mature bone at the periphery and proliferating fibroblasts centrally
Sheets of small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and glycogen
approach: Recall that myositis ossificans matures from the outside in, which is called the zonal pattern.
Its center holds immature, proliferating fibroblasts, the middle zone holds osteoid and woven bone, and the rim holds mature bone.
Osteosarcoma shows the reverse: its most immature, atypical cells are at the edge, invading the tissue around it.
questions.why: Myositis ossificans is a benign reaction to muscle injury in which mesenchymal cells form bone in the muscle. It matures in zones. The center is cellular, with fibroblast-like cells that can look busy, the middle zone has osteoid and woven bone, and the periphery has the most mature bone, which is why the radiograph shows a mineralized rim. Osteosarcoma is the reverse: it may be most mineralized centrally, and its atypical cells make malignant osteoid that infiltrates the surrounding muscle. Recognizing this zonal pattern prevents an unnecessary radical operation.
whyNot: Malignant osteoid infiltrating the surrounding muscle is the hallmark of osteosarcoma.
Mature bone centrally with atypical cells at the edges is the reverse zonal pattern, which points to osteosarcoma.
Correct.
Small round blue cells with glycogen describe Ewing sarcoma, which usually arises in the shaft of a long bone or the pelvis.

questions.stem: A lesion of the nerve that supplies the injured muscle, just below the inguinal ligament, would most likely cause which of the following?
options: Weak knee extension with numbness over the medial leg
Weak hip adduction with numbness over the medial thigh
Foot drop with numbness over the dorsum of the foot
Contralateral pelvic drop during stance on the affected leg
approach: The vastus intermedius is part of the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve.
The quadriceps extends the knee, so femoral nerve injury weakens knee extension and reduces the patellar reflex.
Its sensory branches cover the anterior thigh, and its saphenous branch covers the medial leg.
questions.why: The femoral nerve (L2 to L4) enters the thigh under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery, and supplies the quadriceps and sartorius. Injury there weakens knee extension, so the knee may buckle, and reduces the patellar reflex. Its anterior cutaneous branches supply the front of the thigh, and its saphenous branch supplies the skin of the medial leg and foot.
whyNot: Correct.
Weak adduction with medial thigh numbness follows obturator nerve injury, which supplies the medial compartment of the thigh.
Foot drop with dorsal foot numbness follows common fibular nerve injury, often at the fibular neck.
A pelvic drop on the opposite side during stance is the Trendelenburg sign of superior gluteal nerve injury, from weak gluteus medius and minimus.

questions.stem: In this lesion, mesenchymal progenitor cells in the injured muscle differentiate into osteoblasts under the control of a master transcription factor. Haploinsufficiency of that same transcription factor causes which of the following conditions?
options: Achondroplasia with shortening of proximal limbs
Osteogenesis imperfecta with blue sclerae and fractures
Campomelic dysplasia with bowed long bones
Cleidocranial dysplasia with absent clavicles
approach: Name the master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation: RUNX2.
Recall what happens when one copy of RUNX2 is lost.
Too little RUNX2 impairs intramembranous bone in particular, giving cleidocranial dysplasia.
questions.why: RUNX2 switches mesenchymal cells into the osteoblast lineage and turns on bone matrix genes. Losing one copy (haploinsufficiency) leaves too little RUNX2 for normal bone formation, which shows most in bones formed by intramembranous ossification, such as the clavicles and skull vault. The result is cleidocranial dysplasia, with absent or small clavicles, delayed closure of the fontanelles and sutures, and dental anomalies. SOX9 plays the matching role for chondrocytes.
whyNot: Achondroplasia comes from a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, which slows chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate.
Osteogenesis imperfecta comes from mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, the genes for type I collagen.
Campomelic dysplasia comes from haploinsufficiency of SOX9, the master transcription factor for chondrocytes.
Correct.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the middle zone of the lesion shows osteoblasts rapidly laying down new bone on strands of osteoid. Which of the following best describes the structure of this newly formed bone?
options: Lamellar bone with osteons around central Haversian canals
Woven bone with haphazard collagen fibers and many osteocytes
Hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae and type II collagen
Spongy lamellar bone with trabeculae surrounding red marrow
approach: Bone that forms quickly, as in repair, the embryo, or reactive lesions, is laid down first as woven bone.
Woven bone has randomly arranged collagen and many large osteocytes and is weaker than lamellar bone.
Over months it is remodeled into lamellar bone, which is organized into osteons in compact bone.
questions.why: Whenever bone forms fast, osteoblasts lay down woven bone: collagen fibers run in random directions, osteocytes are numerous and irregular, and the bone is mechanically weak. Later, it is remodeled into lamellar bone, in which collagen runs in parallel layers. In compact bone the lamellae wrap around Haversian canals to form osteons, linked by Volkmann canals, and in spongy bone they form trabeculae around marrow. The middle zone of a lesion only weeks old is still making woven bone.
whyNot: Osteons with Haversian canals are the mature lamellar structure of compact bone. They take months to form by remodeling.
Correct.
Cartilage may appear in some lesions, but the stem describes bone being formed, and the earliest bone is woven.
Spongy bone is also lamellar and mature. It is not the first bone laid down in a reactive lesion.

case: A 62-year-old woman with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the physician because of two episodes of cellulitis in the past year and increasing fatigue. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Examination shows symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints with sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints, ulnar deviation of the fingers, swan-neck deformities, and firm subcutaneous nodules over both olecranon processes. The spleen is palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0), leukocyte count is 2,600/mm3 (normal 4,500 to 11,000), absolute neutrophil count is 700/mm3 (normal 1,500 to 8,000), and platelet count is 198,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are positive. Diagnosis: rheumatoid arthritis with Felty syndrome.

questions.stem: She carries HLA-DRB1*04 (HLA-DR4) alleles, whose shared epitope binds certain modified self-peptides especially well and presents them to CD4 T cells. Her antibodies target the same modified peptides. Which of the following posttranslational modifications creates these self-peptides?
options: Hydroxylation of lysine residues by lysyl hydroxylase
Enzymatic conversion of arginine residues to citrulline
Phosphorylation of tyrosine residues by receptor kinases
Deamidation of glutamine residues by tissue transglutaminase
approach: Link the anti-CCP antibody to its target: proteins containing citrulline.
Citrulline is made after translation when peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes convert arginine residues.
HLA-DR4 shared epitope alleles present citrullinated peptides well, which drives T cell help for autoantibody production.
questions.why: Inflammation, and in the lungs smoking, activates peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes that convert arginine residues in proteins such as fibrinogen, vimentin, and collagen into citrulline. In people with HLA-DR4 shared epitope alleles, these citrullinated peptides fit well into the MHC class II groove and activate CD4 T cells. The T cells help B cells make anti-CCP antibodies and drive synovitis through TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. The inflamed synovium becomes pannus, and RANKL-activated osteoclasts erode cartilage and bone.
whyNot: Lysine hydroxylation is a normal step in collagen synthesis that allows cross-linking. It is not the target of rheumatoid arthritis autoantibodies.
Correct.
Tyrosine phosphorylation is a signaling step in receptor tyrosine kinase pathways. It does not create the rheumatoid autoantigens.
Glutamine deamidation by tissue transglutaminase creates gliadin peptides that bind HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 in celiac disease.

questions.stem: Her sister has hand osteoarthritis. Which of the following radiographic findings in this patient's hands would best distinguish her disease from her sister's?
options: Osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis with asymmetric joint space loss
Pencil-in-cup deformities with fluffy periosteal new bone
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges of cortical bone
Marginal bony erosions with periarticular osteopenia
approach: Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory synovitis, and osteoarthritis is degeneration of cartilage with bony overgrowth.
Inflamed synovium erodes bone at the joint margins where cartilage does not cover it, and cytokines thin the nearby bone.
Osteoarthritis builds bone, with osteophytes and sclerosis, instead of eroding it.
questions.why: In rheumatoid arthritis, pannus first attacks the bare areas at the joint margins, where bone sits inside the capsule without cartilage cover, producing marginal erosions. Cytokines and disuse thin the bone around the joint, which is periarticular osteopenia. Joint space narrowing is even across the joint, and the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints are hit symmetrically, with the distal joints spared. Osteoarthritis instead shows uneven joint space loss, subchondral sclerosis, cysts, and osteophytes, often at the distal interphalangeal joints.
whyNot: Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and uneven narrowing are the features of osteoarthritis, her sister's disease.
Pencil-in-cup deformities with periosteal new bone are typical of psoriatic arthritis, which favors the distal interphalangeal joints.
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges are the classic radiographic sign of chronic tophaceous gout.
Correct.

questions.stem: She also reports 2 years of gritty, dry eyes and a dry mouth that makes it hard to swallow crackers. Which of the following autoantibodies, if present, would most support the additional diagnosis suggested by these symptoms?
options: Anti-SSA/Ro
Anti-Jo-1
Anti-Scl-70
Anti-Smith
approach: Dry eyes and dry mouth point to Sjogren syndrome, which often occurs secondary to rheumatoid arthritis.
Match Sjogren syndrome to its autoantibodies: anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La).
Rule out antibodies tied to myositis, diffuse scleroderma, and SLE.
questions.why: Sjogren syndrome is lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. It can occur alone or alongside rheumatoid arthritis and other connective tissue diseases. Anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies support the diagnosis. Anti-SSA also matters in pregnancy, because it crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-Jo-1 is linked to inflammatory myositis, often with interstitial lung disease.
Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is linked to diffuse systemic sclerosis.
Anti-Smith is highly specific for SLE.

questions.stem: In her metacarpophalangeal joints, inflamed synovium has spread over the surface of the articular cartilage as pannus. The cartilage beneath it thins even in areas without direct erosion. Which of the following normally supplies nutrients to this articular cartilage?
options: Capillaries running through the articular cartilage matrix
Lymphatic vessels in the deep calcified cartilage layer
Diffusion from the synovial fluid in the joint cavity
Perichondrial vessels covering the articular surface
approach: Recall that articular hyaline cartilage has no blood vessels, nerves, lymphatics, or perichondrium.
Its chondrocytes get nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid, helped by joint loading and movement.
Pannus covering the surface blocks this supply and releases enzymes, so the cartilage starves and breaks down.
questions.why: Synovial joints are lined by a synovial membrane whose cells make synovial fluid, rich in hyaluronan and lubricin. The articular surface is hyaline cartilage with no blood supply and no perichondrium, so its chondrocytes depend on diffusion of nutrients from this fluid, pumped in and out as the joint is loaded. In rheumatoid arthritis, pannus spreading over the cartilage cuts off this diffusion and releases proteases and cytokines, so the cartilage degrades even before the bone is eroded.
whyNot: Articular cartilage is avascular. It has no capillaries in its matrix, which is one reason it heals poorly.
Cartilage has no lymphatic vessels. The calcified deep layer anchors it to bone.
Correct.
Articular cartilage has no perichondrium, unlike most other hyaline cartilage, such as the cartilage of the trachea.

case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of heartburn and difficulty swallowing solid food. For 8 years, her fingers have turned white, then blue, then red when exposed to cold. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Examination shows thickened, tight, shiny skin of the fingers distal to the metacarpophalangeal joints and around the mouth, with no skin thickening on the arms or trunk. There are telangiectasias on the face and lips, small firm white nodules at the fingertips, and healed pitted scars on several fingertips. Antinuclear antibody testing is positive at a titer of 1:640. Esophageal manometry shows weak peristalsis in the distal esophagus and a low lower esophageal sphincter pressure. Diagnosis: limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).

questions.stem: Over the next several years, which of the following changes in her hands is most likely to develop?
options: Ulnar deviation with erosions at the metacarpophalangeal joints
Reducible deformities without erosions from lax tendons
Bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints
Fixed flexion contractures of the fingers from skin fibrosis
approach: Identify the disease process: fibrosis of the skin and tissues around the joints, with Raynaud phenomenon and calcinosis.
Tight, thickened skin and fibrotic tissue over the fingers cannot stretch.
The fingers become fixed in flexion: sclerodactyly with flexion contractures.
questions.why: In systemic sclerosis, activated fibroblasts lay down excess collagen in the skin and in tendon sheaths and joint capsules. Over the fingers this produces sclerodactyly, and as the tissues tighten the fingers are pulled into fixed flexion contractures. Calcinosis deposits form at the fingertips, and ischemia from Raynaud phenomenon leaves pitted scars or ulcers. Joint involvement is usually from this fibrosis rather than erosive synovitis.
whyNot: Ulnar deviation with marginal erosions is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, an erosive synovitis.
Reducible deformities without erosions from lax tendons and capsules are typical of SLE arthritis (Jaccoud arthropathy).
Bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden nodes) is a sign of osteoarthritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Given the limited distribution of her skin thickening and her other findings, which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be found on further testing?
options: Anti-Jo-1
Anticentromere
Anti-topoisomerase I
Anti-U1 RNP
approach: Separate the two forms of systemic sclerosis by skin extent: limited (distal limbs and face) and diffuse (proximal limbs and trunk).
Limited disease with calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia is CREST.
Anticentromere antibodies go with the limited form; anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) goes with the diffuse form.
questions.why: Systemic sclerosis is split by how far the skin thickening extends. In the limited form, skin changes stay distal to the elbows and knees and on the face, the course is slow, and anticentromere antibodies are typical. The major late risk is pulmonary arterial hypertension. In the diffuse form, skin thickens on the upper arms and trunk early, anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies are typical, and interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis are more common.
whyNot: Anti-Jo-1 is linked to inflammatory myositis with interstitial lung disease and mechanic's hands.
Correct.
Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) is linked to diffuse systemic sclerosis, with skin thickening on the trunk and proximal limbs.
Anti-U1 RNP is linked to mixed connective tissue disease, which combines features of SLE, scleroderma, and myositis.

questions.stem: During an attack of Raynaud phenomenon, cold increases sympathetic alpha-1 adrenergic constriction of her digital arteries. Vascular smooth muscle can hold this contraction for long periods while using far less ATP than skeletal muscle needs to hold the same force. Which of the following best explains this economy of energy?
options: Calcium binding to troponin C to keep myosin-binding sites exposed
Rigor cross-bridges that persist because cellular ATP is depleted
Latch-state cross-bridges that detach slowly after dephosphorylation
Rising myosin light chain kinase activity throughout the contraction
approach: Note the clue: force held for a long time with little ATP use.
Recall that smooth muscle can keep its force after the myosin light chains have been dephosphorylated.
Dephosphorylated myosin heads still bound to actin detach very slowly, which is the latch state, so tension is held at low energy cost.
questions.why: Smooth muscle starts contracting when calcium binds calmodulin and the complex activates myosin light chain kinase. The kinase phosphorylates the regulatory light chain, and myosin begins cycling on actin. Once force has built up, myosin light chain phosphatase can remove the phosphate from heads that are still attached to actin. These heads detach very slowly, so they keep holding tension while using little ATP. This is the latch state, and it lets vascular smooth muscle maintain tone for long periods at a low energy cost. In systemic sclerosis, damaged and narrowed digital arteries make this normal cold response severe enough to cause ulcers and pitted scars.
whyNot: Smooth muscle has no troponin. Calcium acts through calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase instead.
Rigor bonds form only when ATP runs out, as after death. Her smooth muscle has ATP and relaxes when the stimulus ends.
Correct.

Light chain kinase activity and light chain phosphorylation fall during a sustained contraction even though force is maintained. That fall is part of the latch state, so rising kinase activity does not explain the low ATP use.

questions.stem: A skin biopsy from her finger shows a thickened dermis packed with dense collagen bundles that have replaced hair follicles and sweat glands. Which of the following collagen types makes up the majority of this excess collagen?
options: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
approach: Recognize the dense dermal collagen as fibrosis from activated fibroblasts.
Recall which collagen makes up most of normal dermis, tendon, and mature scar: type I.
Fibroblasts in systemic sclerosis overproduce the same dermal collagen, so type I dominates.
questions.why: Type I collagen is the main collagen of dermis, bone, tendon, ligament, and mature scar, and it forms thick, strong fibers. In systemic sclerosis, TGF-beta and other signals drive fibroblasts to make far too much collagen, and the dermis fills with dense type I bundles that crowd out skin appendages. Type III collagen is also increased, especially early, but type I makes up most of the excess.
whyNot: Correct.
Type II collagen is found in hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus. It is not a skin collagen.
Type III collagen rises in early fibrosis and in granulation tissue, but it makes up a smaller share than type I.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes, such as those under the epidermis and around vessels. It does not fill the dermis.
